I.  General principles of antibiotic therapy
Treatment of infections due to Gram-negative bacilli: Gram negative bacilli are intrinsically resistant
to penicillin. However, the majority of gram-negative bacilli were originally susceptible to extended
spectrum penicillins (ampicillin, amoxicillin, piperacillin) as well as cephalosporins. Later, these
bacteria started producing road spectrum beta lactamases. These beta lactamases inactivate
extended spectrum penicillins and first generation cephalosporins as well as some second
generation cephalosporins. However, third and fourth generation cephalosporins are resistant to the
action of these beta lactamases. So, the drugs of choice for these pathogens were 3rd or 4th
generation cephalosporins. However, of late the emergence of very broad-spectrum beta lactamases
has increasingly rendered 3rd and 4th generation cephalosporins largely ineffective against Gram
negative bacilli

Gram negative bacilli are important pathogens in UTI and intra-abdominal infections. They are
usually caused by enteric Gram-negative bacilli such as E coli, Klebsiella etc. Over 3/4th of even
community acquired enteric Gram-negative bacilli produce ESBL; 3rd or 4th generation cephalosporins
are ineffective against such bacteria. Such infections should be treated with BL/BLI or carbapenems.
BL/BLI combinations are generally effective, but they may be inferior to carbapenems in severe or
life-threatening infections, particularly in high inoculum infections.

classes of antibiotics as well. They are commonly resistant to cotrimoxazole and quinolones.

classes of antibiotics as well. They are commonly resistant to cotrimoxazole and quinolones.
However, the vast majority of community acquired ESBL producing gram negative bacilli remain
susceptible to amikacin.

Carbapenems are not inactivated by extended spectrum or Amp C beta lactamases. They are
effective against even ESBL or Amp C producing bacteria. However, carbapenemase producing gram
negative bacilli are increasing in prevalence, and we are beginning to lose these potent weapons as
well. This is gradually leading us to a post-antibiotic era ruled by superbugs.

Note: Beta lactamase inhibitors have only limited efficacy against Amp C beta lactamases; hence
BL/BLI combinations do not work well against Amp C producing bacteria

ESBL coverage is not required for community acquired infections above diaphragm, such as
meningitis and pneumonia. There, BL/BLI or carbapenems are generally not required; 3rd generation
cephalosporins remain the choice.

Other antibiotics for infections with gram negative bacilli (irrespective of beta lactamase
production): Even though originally cotrimoxazole was a very effective antibiotic against many gram-
negative bacilli, well over 2/3rd of even community acquired E. coli and Klebsiella isolates are now
resistant to co-trimoxazole.

Similarly, originally quinolones had excellent activity against most of the gram-negative bacilli, but
now well over 2/3rd of even community acquired gram negative bacilli are quinolone resistant.
Gentamicin resistance is common even among community acquired pathogens but most of the
community acquired gram negative bacilli (>90%) remain susceptible to amikacin. However,
amikacin resistance is becoming increasingly common among hospital acquired gram negative bacilli.

Staphylococcal infections: Once upon a time,
Staph. aureus strains were fully susceptible to penicillin. But over the years, they started producing
penicillinase which inactivates penicillin and its broad spectrum and extended spectrum derivatives
such as ampicillin, amoxicillin, and piperacillin. Now over 90% of the strains are resistant to
penicillin. To overcome this problem, penicillinase resistant penicillins were developed. They are
resistant to the action of penicillinase. This group is called the methicillin group and includes
methicillin, oxacillin, cloxacillin, dicloxacillin, flucloxacillin and nafcillin. Methicillin is no longer used
clinically. Only cloxacillin and flucloxacillin are available in India.  It must be noted that the
staphylococcal penicillinase is a narrow spectrum penicillinase and does not inactivate
cephalosporins and BL/BLI combinations. So, drugs of choice for staphylococci today are penicillinase
resistant penicillins, cephalosporins and BL/BLI combinations. Since these staphylococci are
susceptible to methicillin, they are called MSSA.

Among cephalosporins, first generation cephalosporins are highly effective against MSSA. Many
second generation cephalosporins and the third generation cephalosporins have only modest
efficacy. Cefepime, the 4th generation cephalosporin and carbapenems also have modest activity

resistant penicillins, cephalosporins and BL/BLI combinations. Since these staphylococci are
susceptible to methicillin, they are called MSSA.

Among cephalosporins, first generation cephalosporins are highly effective against MSSA. Many
second generation cephalosporins and the third generation cephalosporins have only modest
efficacy. Cefepime, the 4th generation cephalosporin and carbapenems also have modest activity
against staphylococci. Some third generation cephalosporins such as cefixime and ceftazidime have
very poor activity against staphylococci.

In the last several decades, staphylococci with altered penicillin binding protein (PBP) have emerged.
Since the binding site is altered, none of the beta lactams are effective against these staphylococci.
These strains are resistant to all beta lactams including the methicillin group, cephalosporins,

carbapenems as well as BL/BLI combinations. They are called MRSA. (Recently some fifth generation
cephalosporins have been developed which are effective against MRSA).

Since penicillinase production and altered PBP affect only beta lactams, they do not influence the
efficacy of other classes of antibiotics against Staphylococci. However, resistance to other classes of
antibiotics such as macrolides, tetracyclines, cotrimoxazole, clindamycin and quinolones has become
increasingly common among both MSSA and MRSA due to different resistant mechanisms. This is
particularly true for MRSA.

Treatment of MSSA: Amoxicillin is ineffective against staphylococci. Cloxacillin and amoxycillin-
clavulanate are effective against MSSA. Other BL/BLI combinations such as ampicillin/sulbactam,
piperacillin/tazobactam and cefoperazone sulbactam are also active against staphylococci. First
generation cephalosporins (cephalexin, cefazolin) are effective against MSSA. In contrast, second
generation and third generation cephalosporins are less effective against staphylococci and are not
the preferred agents. Cefixime, an oral third generation cephalosporin has very poor anti-
staphylococcal effect.

Other antibiotics which were originally effective against staphylococci (both MSSA and MRSA)
include tetracyclines, clindamycin, macrolides, cotrimoxazole, quinolones. They can be used for non-
serious infections. However, resistance has become common for macrolides, quinolones,
cotrimoxazole and to a lesser extent clindamycin.

may still be clindamycin resistant due to a phenomenon called inducible clindamycin resistance.

MIC is a measure of sensitivity of bacteria to antibiotics. The success of therapy depends on the MIC
of the strain as well as the site of infection and the dose and route of the antibiotic.

Treatment of meningitis: Penicillin penetrates the uninflamed meninges poorly. CSF level of penicillin
is only 0.02% of that of plasma, increasing to 20% with strong meningeal inflammation. Levels
achieved in CSF are sufficient to kill the bacteria only if the MIC of the strain is very low (≤0.06
µg/mL). If the MIC is ≥0.12 µg/mL or above, penicillin becomes ineffective.

Treatment of infections outside the CNS with IV therapy: For infections outside CNS such as
pneumonia, IV penicillin G is effective as long as the MIC of the strain is ≤4 µg/mL.

Oral therapy for otitis media, sinusitis and CAP: Since oral therapy can achieve only much lower
plasma levels, oral therapy is effective only if the MIC is low; strains with MIC of ≤0.06 µg/mL are
considered susceptible and respond to usual doses of amoxicillin (500 mg tid in adults and
45mg/kg/day in children); strains with MIC of 0.12 to 1 µg/mL are considered intermediate and
respond to double the usual doses of amoxicillin (1000 mg tid or 90mg/kg/day in children). Strains
with MIC of 2 µg/mL or above will not respond to oral therapy.

ICMR AMR surveillance data for the year 2021 shows that, among meningeal isolates penicillin
susceptibility is only 23% and ceftriaxone susceptibility is only 67%. So, empiric therapy for
community acquired pyogenic meningitis should be ceftriaxone with vancomycin. The same data
showed that penicillin and ceftriaxone susceptibility among non-meningeal invasive isolates was 98%

is highly effective, and addition of vancomycin is generally not warranted.

Oral therapy for otitis media, sinusitis, and CAP: The usual dose of amoxicillin for the above
infections is 500 mg tid in adults and 45 mg/kg/day in children. Such a dose is effective only if the
MIC of the strain is 0.06 µg/mL or less. However, pneumococci with intermediate penicillin
resistance (MIC of 0.12-1 µg/mL) have become increasingly common in India. For the outpatient
treatment of CAP or sinusitis or otitis media due to such strains, usual dose of amoxicillin is
ineffective and double the usual doses are recommended. Oral third generation cephalosporins such
as cefpodoxime or cefdinir are also effective but high dose amoxicillin remains the most effective
oral beta lactam against these strains. Resistance in pneumococci is due to modification of the
binding site and not due to production of beta lactamase; hence, BL/BLI combinations offer no
advantage against pneumococci as compared to BL alone.

II. Principles of treatment of infection and sepsis
Treatment of infection vs sepsis: It is important to differentiate infection from sepsis. Sepsis refers
to infection leading to life threatening organ dysfunction; it is a medical emergency; antibiotics need
to be started as soon as possible ideally within one hour. However, infection without organ
dysfunction is usually not a medical emergency.

Sepsis = infection + life threatening organ dysfunction caused by infection

Infection vs sepsis: In the early stages of infection, the organ function is normal, but over time, the
interplay of infection and host response may lead to organ dysfunction. Note that even when
infection is accompanied by bacteraemia there is no organ dysfunction in the early stages, but
untreated infection and bacteraemia can potentially lead to organ dysfunction. When infection leads
to organ dysfunction, it is called sepsis. Organ dysfunction is usually the result of dysregulated host
response. Whether infection proceeds to sepsis/organ dysfunction depends on several factors such
as virulence of the pathogen, microbial load, immune status of the host, physiological reserve of the
host, co-morbidities etc. Source control and effective antimicrobial therapy can prevent or limit the
organ dysfunction. Development of sepsis/organ dysfunction significantly increases morbidity and
mortality; so, it is critically important that sepsis is recognized early and treated effectively.

There are two approaches to antibiotic therapy:
     De-escalation approach: Start with broad spectrum and or combination therapy and deescalate
after culture reports or clinical improvement. This approach should be limited for serious or life-
threatening situations where inappropriate empirical therapy has serious consequences.

     Escalation approach: Start with limited spectrum antibiotic appropriate for the infection;
Switch to broader spectrum drug or add additional drugs only if initial therapy fails. This approach is
appropriate for mild to moderate infections where failure of initial therapy does not have serious
consequences. This helps in limiting the use of broad spectrum and reserve drugs.

So, it is important to strike a balance between the need to provide appropriate empirical therapy
and the need to minimize the use of broad spectrum and reserve drugs.

Sepsis represents medical emergency and needs to be treated aggressively; broad spectrum

III. Getting your antibiotic right
Empirical therapy vs definitive therapy: In patients with infection, we start antibiotics after sending
cultures. The initial choice of antibiotics depends on several factors such as site of infection, severity
of illness, place of acquisition, host factors, etc. This is called empirical therapy. Once culture
reports become available, the antibiotics are adjusted as per the organism and sensitivity pattern.
Such culture guided therapy is called definitive therapy.

The 5 Rs of antibiotic therapy: The clinician should make every attempt to ensure all the following
                         •   Right diagnosis (The ID syndrome)
                         •   Right drug
                         •   Right time
                         •   Right dose
                         •   Right duration

Right diagnosis (identifying the ID syndrome)

Right diagnosis is extremely important. First, we need to identify the focus of infection or the ID
syndrome. This is primarily based on history and physical examination. It is supplemented by initial
laboratory tests that are immediately available. Based on the ID syndrome, the necessary samples
must be sent; making the microbiological diagnosis is crucial. As additional test results become
available the ID syndrome should be further defined.

Other cultures: Send other relevant cultures based on the suspected source (eg. urine, sputum, pus
etc.)

Urine culture: Urine sample for culture should be processed immediately (within 1 to 2 hours).
Otherwise, it may be refrigerated at 4 degree C up to 24 hours; but once removed from
refrigeration, it should be processed immediately.

of antibiotic therapy significantly increases mortality. Inappropriate initial empiric therapy also

administration of appropriate initial empirical antibiotic therapy.

Right drug: Administering appropriate empirical therapy is crucial. Mortality significantly increases
with inappropriate therapy. Several factors should be considered in the selection of empiric therapy.
It should cover the likely pathogens. Which pathogens need to be covered depends on several
factors. First and foremost, we should identify the focus of infection or the ID syndrome (UTI,
pneumonia, meningitis, etc). Next, we should consider the site of acquisition of infection and the
local prevalence of antibiotic resistance in the community, hospital, or the unit under consideration.
Among community acquired infections, recent hospitalization of at least 5 days within the last 90

days and recent use of parenteral antibiotics within the last 90 days increase the risk of resistant
pathogens. Resistant pathogens are more likely in hospital acquired infections, particularly with ICU
acquired infections as compared to ward acquired infections. Immune status of the patient strongly
influences the likely pathogens and the need for aggressive therapy. Factors such as the presence of
central venous catheters etc increase the probability of Staphylococcal infection. It is important to
consider the entry of the selected drug into the relevant compartment. For example,
aminoglycosides do not enter the CNS and hence should not be used to cover Gram negative
meningitis; neonates with immature blood brain barrier are an exception.

Factors influencing the choice of empiric therapy:
          1. source of infection (ID syndrome)
          2. severity of illness
          3. community or hospital acquired (ward acquired, or ICU acquired in case of later)
          4. local prevalence of resistant pathogens in the community/hospital/unit
          5. risk factors for MDR pathogens in the individual (recent antibiotic use, recent
             hospitalization, prior colonization/infection with MDR pathogens)
          6. presence of devices (urinary catheter, central venous catheter etc)
          7. adequateness of source control, in applicable patients
          8. age, comorbidity
          9. immunocompetent vs compromised.
         10.renal or liver disease (safety as well as need for dose adjustment)

Empirical therapy vs definitive therapy: In patients with infection, we start antibiotics after sending
cultures. The initial choice of antibiotics depends on several factors such as site of infection, severity

aminoglycoside is often added as a second antibiotic to provide additional coverage against gram
negative bacilli. Vancomycin may be added if there is a need to provide MRSA coverage.

Gastrointestinal Infections – Diarrhoea – General Principles
Definition: Diarrhoea is defined as the passage of loose or watery stools, typically at least three times in a 24-hour period.
Acute diarrhoea is defined as diarrhoea of ≤14 days in duration, in contrast to persistent (>14 days and ≤30 days) or chronic (>30 days) diarrhoea.
Dysentery is defined as diarrhoea with visible blood is stools. Dysentery is commonly associated with fever and abdominal pain.
   ●   Mild diarrhoea (<3 unformed stools/day, minimal associated symptomatology).
   ●  Moderate diarrhoea (3 to 6 unformed stools/day &/or systemic symptoms)
   ●   Severe diarrhoea (>6 unformed stools/day, temp >101°F, tenesmus, blood in stool, or faecal leukocytes)

Microbiology
Common pathogens in acute community-acquired diarrhoea: Rotavirus, Norovirus, Salmonella, Shigella, enterotoxigenic E. coli, Campylobacter; consider V. cholera in outbreaks.
Consider acute gastroenteritis due to preformed toxin as well (prominent vomiting is usual; Bacillus cereus, Staphylococcus aureus and Clostridium perfringens).
Nosocomial diarrhoea: C. difficile
Persistent diarrhoea in immunocompromised (most likely causes vary depending on type of immunocompromise): Giardia, Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Isospora, Microsporidia,
Cytomegalovirus.

Symptomatic therapy
Antimotility drug: Loperamide may be used for rapid control of symptoms. It can be used for mild to-moderate diarrhoea but should be avoided in inflammatory diarrhoea (do not
give if there is fever, significant abdominal pain, or bloody stools)
Antibiotic therapy
Carefully assess the patient before prescribing antimicrobials. Most infectious diarrhoea is self-limited and only requires supportive management.
Treatment with antibiotics is not recommended for most mild & moderate disease. Antibiotic use may lead to adverse outcomes (e.g. 20 fold higher risk of HUS with Shiga toxin-
producing E. Coli, increased risk of chronic carrier state in NTS infection). Viral pathogens, such as Rotavirus and Norovirus commonly cause diarrhoea and do not require
antibiotics. A significant proportion of diarrhoea is due to viral pathogens (rotavirus in children and Norovirus in adults).

Non bloody diarrhoea

Carefully assess the patient before prescribing antimicrobials. Most infectious diarrhoea is self-limited and only requires supportive management.
Treatment with antibiotics is not recommended for most mild & moderate disease. Antibiotic use may lead to adverse outcomes (e.g. 20 fold higher risk of HUS with Shiga toxin-
producing E. Coli, increased risk of chronic carrier state in NTS infection). Viral pathogens, such as Rotavirus and Norovirus commonly cause diarrhoea and do not require
antibiotics. A significant proportion of diarrhoea is due to viral pathogens (rotavirus in children and Norovirus in adults).

Non bloody diarrhoea
Frequently self-limiting and may not be bacterial. Antibacterial not usually indicated. Antibiotic is indicated only in severe disease. Empirical therapy may be justified in patients
with high fever, significant abdominal pain, persistent or worsening symptoms. However high fever and significant abdominal pain occur in viral diarrhoea also (rotavirus or
norovirus)
Consider acute gastroenteritis due to preformed toxin as well (prominent vomiting is usual; Bacillus cereus, Staphylococcus aureus and Clostridium perfringens).
Bloody stools with fever
Patients with bloody stools and fever require antibiotics (indicates infection with Shigella, entero-invasive E. coli, Campylobacter, Yersinia, or Vibrio parahaemolyticus; Clostridium
difficile is also a consideration). Amoebic dysentery is also a consideration.
Bloody stools without fever
Consider enterohaemorrhagic E. coli; avoid antibiotics as they increase the risk of HUS by 20-fold. Consider amoebic dysentery (as only < 40% of patients have fever).

● Cellulitis is an acute spreading infection of the skin that involves the subcutaneous tissues.
● Predisposing factors: previous trauma, often minor (laceration, abrasion, puncture wound) or underlying skin lesion (furuncle, ulcer, dermatophyte infection)
● Involvement is often extensive, with marked erythema, warmth, and swelling.
● Regional lymphadenopathy is common, and bacteraemia can occur.
● Local abscesses may develop, and small patches of overlying skin may subsequently undergo necrosis.
● Two types of cellulitis exist. Non-suppurative cellulitis and suppurative cellulitis
● A nidus of suppuration with surrounding cellulitis (suppurative cellulitis) is a hallmark of staphylococcal cellulitis, although this diagnostic finding is not always
  present.
● Always elevate affected extremity. Not elevating the limb often leads to treatment failure.
● Improvement of erythema can take days, especially in patients with lymphedema, because dead bacteria in the tissues continue to induce Inflammation.
● Very early post-operative wound infection within 6 to 48 hours after surgery is characteristic of streptococcal infection; in contrast, postoperative
  staphylococcal infection will not be evident for at least several days after surgery.
● Neutropenic, solid organ transplant, and cirrhotic patients may have cellulitis due to Gram-negative organisms. Consider expanding coverage in these cases.

Skin and Soft Tissue Infections – Diabetic Foot

Diabetic foot infection:
Look for evidence of infection (features of inflammation or purulence)
Non infected ulcers do not need antibiotics
Cultures should not be taken from clinically non-infected wounds
If there is evidence of infection, then antibiotics are indicated depending on the severity
(see international working group on diabetic foot classifications in the table)

Establishing the pathogen
Deep tissue specimens, obtained aseptically at surgery, usually contain only the true pathogens.
Material obtained through curettage (tissue scraping) with a curette or scalpel from the base of a debrided ulcer or needle aspirate of purulent secretions are
reasonable alternatives.
Swabs of superficial lesions often yield contaminants.
If swabs are the only available method, they should be taken only after debriding and cleaning the wound.

Acute infections in previously untreated patients are usually caused by aerobic gram-positive cocci (often as a monomicrobial infection), but deep or chronic
wounds may harbour polymicrobial flora, including gram-negative and anaerobic bacteria

S. aureus and β-haemolytic streptococci are common pathogens for cellulitis or mildly infected ulcers.

XIII. Bone and Joint Infections
• Hematogenous spread is the most common route in all age groups.
• Arthritis is monoarticular in 80% to 90% of cases. The most common joint affected is the knee in adults. Hip, shoulder, wrist, and ankle are frequently involved.
  In children, hip infections predominate.
• In adults, fever and malaise are common but high fever with rigors and shaking chills are typically not apparent.
• Polyarticular arthritis is observed in 10% to 20% of patients, especially in those with rheumatoid arthritis, immunosuppression, or prolonged or intense
  bacteremia, and is usually caused by S. aureus.
• De-escalate once the causative organism is identified.
• Synovial fluid analysis:
   o  Synovial fluid WBC count of >50,000 WBC/cu.mm has a sensitivity of 62% and specificity of 92%. A synovial fluid WBC count of >25,000 WBC/cmm has a
        higher sensitivity of 77% but lower specificity of 73%.
   o  Synovial fluid culture in patients who have not previously received antibiotics will yield bacterial growth up to 80% to 90% of the time; however, Gram
         staining is diagnostic in only 50% of these cases. False-positive Gram stains of synovial fluid can occur because of artefacts from stain, mucin, and cellular

         1. Polymy ins dosing

There are two polymyxin antibiotics: Colistin also called as Polymyxin E, and Polymyxin B.

Generally, both the polymyxins show poor penetration into the lungs, pleura, bones, and central
nervous system. They are not effective against many Gram-negative pathogens.

Susceptible organisms:

Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, some Enterobacter spp, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and
Acinetobacter baumannii. Other susceptible organisms include Haemophilus influenzae, Bordetella
pertussis, Legionella pneumophila, Salmonella spp, Shigella spp, and the majority of
Stenotrophomonas maltophilia strains. However, acquried resistance in these organisms may lead to
resistance to polymyxins

Resistant organisms:

The following organisms are intrinsically resistant to polymyxins. Proteus spp, Providencia spp,
Serratia marcescens, Morganella morganii, Burkholderia cepacia, Moraxella catarrhalis are all
intrinsically resistant to polymyxins. Organisms with variable resistance include Aeromonas, Vibrio,
Prevotella, and Fusobacterium spp

Polymyxin B is generally preferred over colistin for all indications with the following exceptions.

Serratia marcescens, Morganella morganii, Burkholderia cepacia, Moraxella catarrhalis are all
intrinsically resistant to polymyxins. Organisms with variable resistance include Aeromonas, Vibrio,
Prevotella, and Fusobacterium spp

Polymyxin B is generally preferred over colistin for all indications with the following exceptions.

    •   Urinary tract infections
    •   Adjunctive inhalation therapy for pneumonia caused by MDR gram-negative bacilli.

For all indications other than UTI, Polymyxin B is preferred over colistin because of equivalent
efficacy, faster attainment of target serum concentrations, less inter-patient variability in
pharmacokinetics, no need for dose adjustment in renal impairment and lower risk of renal toxicity.
Polymyxin B achieves adequate plasma levels more rapidly and reliably than colistin. Polymyxin B is
administered as the active agent, whereas colistin is a prodrug that has to be converted to the active
agent.

For UTI, colistin is preferred over polymyxin B; colistin achieves high urinary concentrations but
polymyxin urinary concentrations are low.

For both the polymyxins, treatment of CNS infection requires adjunctive intrathecal therapy;
administration by nebulization should be considered for treatment of pneumonia

Piperacillin (in combination with tazobactam) is excreted mainly in the urine. Peak concentrations are
achieved in the serum immediately following completion of 30-minute infusion.

Both piperacillin and tazobactam are approximately 30% bound to plasma proteins. The protein
binding of either piperacillin or tazobactam is unaffected by the presence of the other compound.
Protein binding of the tazobactam metabolite is negligible. Piperacillin and tazobactam are widely
distributed into tissues and body fluids including intestinal mucosa, gallbladder, lung, female

Piperacillin is metabolized to a minor microbiologically active desethyl metabolite. Tazobactam is
metabolized to a single metabolite that lacks pharmacological and antibacterial activities.

Wound classification:

Clean wounds are uninfected operative wounds in which no inflammation is encountered and the
wound is closed primarily. By definition, a viscus (respiratory, alimentary, genital, or urinary tract) is
not entered during a clean procedure.
Clean-contaminated wounds are operative wounds in which a viscus (respiratory, alimentary, genital,
or urinary tract) is entered under controlled conditions and without unusual contamination.
Contaminated wounds are open, fresh accidental wounds, operations with major breaks in sterile
technique, or gross spillage from a viscus. Wounds in which acute, nonpurulent inflammation was
encountered also were included in this category.
Dirty wounds are old traumatic wounds with retained devitalized tissue, foreign bodies, or fecal
contamination or wounds that involve existing clinical infection or perforated viscus.

Several studies have found a moderate correlation between the wound classification and the SSI rate.
SSI rates according to wound class were:

        Clean                           1.3 to 2.9 %
        Clean-contaminated             2.4 to 7.7 %
        Contaminated                 6.4 to 15.2 %
         Dirty                          7.1 to 40.0 %

Pathogens causing surgical site infection:

The predominant organisms causing SSIs after clean procedures are skin flora, including S. aureus
and coagulase-negative staphylococci (e.g., Staphylococcus epidermidis). In clean-contaminated
procedures, including abdominal procedures and heart, kidney, and liver transplantations, the
predominant organisms include gram-negative rods and enterococci in addition to skin flora.

Choice and the timing of the antibiotic:

Successful prophylaxis requires that

    1.  The antibiotic chosen should cover the pathogens likely to cause surgical site infection
    2.  The timing of administration of the antibiotic should ensure that serum and tissue
       concentrations of the antibiotic exceeds the MIC of organisms at the time of incision and
       the levels should be maintained above MIC throughout the duration of the procedure.
       There is no need to administer the antibiotic once the surgery has been completed.

Timing of the antibiotic:

For antibiotics that are given as IV push over 3 to 5 minutes or as short infusion, the infusion should
be started not earlier than 60 minutes of expected time of surgical incision. The antibiotic
administration infusion should be completed before the surgical incision to ensure that therapeutic
levels of the antibiotic is present in the tissues at the time of skin incision. For antibiotics requiring
prolonged infusion over 1 to 2 hours, such as vancomycin or fluoroquinolones, the infusion should be
started not earlier than 120 minutes prior to the expected time of surgical incision. These drugs have
long half-lives, and they are likely to sustain the levels above MIC for the period of surgery despite
starting the infusions earlier.

Redosing of the antibiotic:

Redosing required depending on the duration of the surgery and the half-life to the drug chosen.
Redosing is also required in the event of major intraoperative blood loss. Redosing may also be
warranted if there are factors that shorten the half-life of the antimicrobial agent (e.g., extensive
burns). The redosing interval should be calculated from the time of administration of the first dose
and not from the time of surgical incision and not from the beginning of the procedure.

For antimicrobials with a short half-life (redosing in the operating room is recommended at an
interval of approximately two times the half-life of the agent in patients with normal renal function.
For example, cefazolin has a half-life of 2 hours, and it should be given every 4 hours, piperacillin
tazobactam has a half-life of 1 hour and should be given every 2 hours.

No further doses are required once the surgery is completed.

Antibiotics with long half-life such as vancomycin do not need redosing.

Despite short half-life, aminoglycosides do not need redosing, because they have prolonged post-

In the event of major intraoperative blood loss additional dosage of prophylactic antibiotic should be
considered after fluid replacement. (>1,500 ml in adults, children >25ml/kg in children is considered
major blood loss). The dose should be repeated after for every 1500 ml blood loss (after fluid
replacement)

Duration of antibiotic prophyla is:

Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis should be generally limited to the duration of the surgery. At any cost,
it should not be continued beyond 24 hours. Pre-operative antibiotic should be continued for several
days only in case of dirty or infected wounds. However, this is treatment of infection and not
prophylaxis. The practice of continuing antimicrobial prophylaxis until all invasive lines, drains, and
indwelling catheters are removed cannot be supported due to concerns regarding the development
of drug-resistant organisms, superinfections, and drug toxicity

Infusion times for antibiotics:

β-lactams (cephalosporins, ampicillin/sulbactam, piperacillin tazobactam): IV push over 3-5 minutes;
all reach adequate skin levels within minutes--hence can be given just before surgery.

Vancomycin: infuse over 60 minutes; start at least 30 minutes before incision

Ciprofloxacin: infuse over 60 minutes

Clindamycin: infuse over 10-20 minutes.

Metronidazole: infuse over 10 minutes.
